PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 147 — Lesson 171: Cardiovascular & Respiratory Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Use symptoms, vital signs, focused examination, ECG, imaging, laboratory data, disease trajectory, and risk to distinguish routine cardiopulmonary care from time-sensitive threats, initiate evidence-based management, and choose a safe disposition.

Learning Objectives

  • Prioritize airway, breathing, circulation, perfusion, and instability before diagnostic detail.
  • Build focused differentials for chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, cough, edema, and exercise intolerance.
  • Differentiate hypertensive emergency from severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage.
  • Recognize acute coronary syndrome, heart failure, dangerous arrhythmia, aortic emergency, pulmonary embolism, severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, and pneumonia red flags.
  • Confirm chronic asthma and COPD using appropriate objective testing when feasible.
  • Integrate cardiovascular and respiratory therapies with kidney function, pregnancy, age, medication safety, and adherence.
  • Use diagnostic stewardship while avoiding false reassurance from a single normal test.
  • Define follow-up, return precautions, referral, and emergency disposition.

Part 1 — One Symptom, Two Interdependent Systems

Dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance, chest discomfort, dizziness, cough, and edema can arise from cardiac, pulmonary, hematologic, metabolic, infectious, medication-related, or mixed causes. The heart delivers blood; the lungs ventilate and oxygenate it. Failure in either system can stress the other.

A patient may have more than one process: COPD plus heart failure, pneumonia triggering atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism causing right-heart strain, or anemia worsening coronary ischemia. Avoid premature closure after finding one familiar diagnosis.

Part 2 — Stability Comes First

Assess airway, work of breathing, respiratory rate, oxygenation in context, mental status, blood pressure, pulse, perfusion, temperature, and ability to speak. Look for cyanosis, silent chest, exhaustion, shock, acute neurologic deficit, ongoing ischemic pain, severe arrhythmia, and pulmonary edema.

Unstable patients require emergency response, stabilization within scope, and transport. Do not delay transfer to finish an outpatient differential or await a low-priority test.

Part 3 — Chest Pain Begins With Can-Not-Miss Diagnoses

Immediate threats include acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, and esophageal rupture. Other causes include pericarditis, pneumonia, pleurisy, reflux, biliary disease, musculoskeletal pain, and anxiety.

Quality alone is unreliable. Burning can be ischemia; tenderness does not fully exclude ACS; absence of classic radiation does not make the case benign. Integrate age, risk, onset, exertion, associated symptoms, vital signs, ECG, and trajectory.

Part 4 — Acute Coronary Syndrome

ACS can present with pressure, tightness, heaviness, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue, arm, shoulder, jaw, back, or upper abdominal discomfort. Older adults, women, and people with diabetes may have less typical descriptions.

Obtain an ECG promptly in an appropriate acute setting and use serial high-sensitivity troponin according to the validated pathway. A single early normal troponin or nondiagnostic ECG does not safely exclude evolving ACS when clinical concern remains. Ongoing or unstable symptoms require emergency evaluation.

Part 5 — Stable Ischemic Symptoms Versus Acute Change

Predictable exertional discomfort relieved by rest suggests a supply-demand pattern from chronic coronary disease, but a new, accelerating, prolonged, or resting pattern raises concern for ACS. Determine functional threshold and change from baseline.

Do not perform routine outpatient stress testing on an unstable patient. After acute disease is excluded, risk-based evaluation and secondary prevention should address lipids, blood pressure, diabetes, tobacco, activity, medication adherence, and cardiac rehabilitation when indicated.

Part 6 — Aortic and Pericardial Clues

Abrupt severe chest or back pain, pulse or blood-pressure asymmetry, neurologic findings, syncope, new aortic regurgitation, or shock raises concern for acute aortic syndrome. Do not use a normal chest radiograph to rule it out.

Pericarditic pain may be sharp, pleuritic, positional, and associated with diffuse ECG changes, but myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and other threats must be considered. Tamponade physiology with hypotension, rising venous pressure, tachycardia, or impaired perfusion is an emergency.

Part 7 — Pulmonary Embolism Is a Probability Problem

Consider recent surgery or immobilization, prior VTE, active cancer, estrogen exposure, pregnancy or postpartum state, unilateral leg findings, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, hemoptysis, and unexplained pleuritic pain or dyspnea.

Use a validated pretest-probability strategy. A rule-out criterion or D-dimer is useful only in the correct population; it should not delay imaging or emergency care when probability and instability are high. Sudden hypotension, severe hypoxemia, syncope, or right-heart strain increases urgency.

Part 8 — A Dyspnea Framework

Classify onset as seconds to minutes, hours to days, or chronic. Ask about exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, sputum, wheeze, fever, chest pain, edema, weight change, exposures, medications, and baseline function.

Examination includes work of breathing, breath sounds, crackles, wheeze, asymmetry, cardiac rhythm, murmurs, jugular venous pressure, edema, perfusion, and signs of anemia or infection. Normal resting oxygen saturation does not exclude exertional disease or serious early pathology.

Part 9 — Measure Blood Pressure Correctly

Use a validated upper-arm device, correct cuff size, proper positioning, rest, repeated measurements, and out-of-office confirmation when appropriate. Review substances and medicines that raise blood pressure and assess adherence and access.

The 2025 multisociety guideline retains adult categories beginning with normal below 120/80 mm Hg, elevated systolic 120–129 with diastolic below 80, stage 1 at 130–139 or 80–89, and stage 2 at 140 or 90 and above. Treatment decisions also incorporate cardiovascular risk and comorbidity.

Part 10 — Severe Hypertension: Look for Acute Organ Injury

A very high number does not by itself define hypertensive emergency. Emergency requires severe hypertension with acute target-organ injury such as encephalopathy, stroke syndrome, ACS, acute pulmonary edema, aortic syndrome, acute kidney injury, or other critical damage.

Severe hypertension without acute organ injury generally requires confirmation, evaluation, oral treatment initiation or intensification, and timely follow-up—not rapid unmonitored normalization. Symptoms or findings of organ injury require emergency transfer and monitored therapy.

Part 11 — Orthostatic Symptoms

Dizziness on standing may reflect volume depletion, medication effect, autonomic dysfunction, blood loss, infection, endocrine disease, deconditioning, or arrhythmia. Measure orthostatic vital signs using a standardized process when safe and interpret them with symptoms.

Review diuretics, vasodilators, alpha blockers, sedatives, and recent changes. In older adults, the therapeutic goal includes fall prevention and function, not only a seated blood-pressure target.

Part 12 — Heart Failure Is a Syndrome

Symptoms include exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, fatigue, edema, abdominal fullness, and weight gain. Findings can include elevated jugular venous pressure, crackles, S3, edema, displaced apical impulse, cool extremities, or hypoperfusion, but absence of one sign does not exclude HF.

Differentiate reduced ejection fraction from preserved ejection fraction using echocardiography and context. Natriuretic peptides can support diagnosis but vary with age, kidney function, rhythm, obesity, and other cardiac stress.

Part 13 — Acute Versus Chronic Heart Failure

Acute pulmonary edema, severe hypoxemia, hypotension, altered mentation, chest pain, new ischemia, rapid arrhythmia, or poor perfusion requires emergency care. Identify triggers such as ischemia, infection, uncontrolled pressure, arrhythmia, medication or dietary change, kidney injury, anemia, or valve disease.

Stable chronic management combines phenotype-specific guideline-directed therapy, volume assessment, kidney and electrolyte monitoring, self-care education, daily trends when useful, vaccination, exercise or rehabilitation, and early response to worsening symptoms.

Part 14 — Palpitations Need Rhythm Documentation

Ask onset, duration, regularity, triggers, abruptness, exercise association, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, stimulant use, thyroid symptoms, family history, and structural disease. Examine pulse and obtain ECG.

Intermittent symptoms may require ambulatory monitoring matched to event frequency. A normal office ECG does not exclude paroxysmal arrhythmia. Palpitations with syncope, ischemic symptoms, severe dyspnea, family history of sudden death, or unstable vital signs increase urgency.

Part 15 — Atrial Fibrillation Requires More Than Rate Control

Confirm the rhythm and assess hemodynamic stability. Then address ventricular rate or rhythm strategy, symptom duration, precipitating illness, structural disease, thyroid or sleep-disordered breathing when relevant, and stroke prevention using a validated risk approach.

Do not assume AF from an irregular pulse alone, and do not prescribe anticoagulation without assessing indication, bleeding risk, interactions, kidney function, adherence, and valve context. Unstable AF requires urgent synchronized management in an appropriate setting.

Part 16 — Syncope Is Transient Cerebral Hypoperfusion

Differentiate syncope from seizure, fall, intoxication, hypoglycemia, stroke mimic, and psychogenic events. History, witness report, orthostatic vitals, cardiac and neurologic examination, medication review, and ECG are central.

Exertional syncope, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death, severe anemia or bleeding, persistent neurologic deficit, chest pain, dyspnea, or injury can signal high risk. Do not label unexplained syncope as vasovagal without supportive features.

Part 17 — Murmurs and Structural Disease

Describe timing, location, radiation, intensity, quality, and associated findings. A harsh systolic murmur radiating to carotids suggests aortic stenosis; a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla suggests mitral regurgitation.

New murmur with dyspnea, syncope, ischemic symptoms, heart failure, fever, embolic signs, or instability warrants expedited evaluation. A new murmur after MI with pulmonary edema raises concern for a mechanical complication and is an emergency.

Part 18 — Edema Is Not Automatically Heart Failure

Consider venous insufficiency, medications, kidney or liver disease, low oncotic pressure, lymphedema, hypothyroidism, DVT, pregnancy, and immobility. Unilateral acute swelling suggests a different process from chronic symmetric dependent edema.

Assess jugular venous pressure, lungs, cardiac findings, weight trend, urine protein, kidney and liver context, medications, skin, and thrombosis risk. Treat the mechanism rather than prescribing a diuretic reflexively.

Part 19 — Asthma Requires Variable Airflow Evidence

Asthma presents with variable wheeze, dyspnea, chest tightness, or cough and variable expiratory airflow limitation. Confirm objectively with spirometry and bronchodilator response or another accepted method when feasible; repeat testing during symptoms if initial results are nondiagnostic.

Consider mimics such as inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, COPD, foreign body, bronchiectasis, GERD-related symptoms, medication effect, and anxiety. A normal examination between episodes is common.

Part 20 — Asthma Control, Risk, and Severity Differ

Control reflects recent symptoms, night waking, reliever use, and activity limitation. Future risk includes prior severe exacerbation, poor lung function, smoking or vaping, poor adherence, incorrect technique, high reliever reliance, eosinophilic inflammation, and comorbidity.

Severity is judged retrospectively by treatment required for control. Before stepping up, confirm diagnosis, inhaler technique, adherence, exposure, and comorbidities. Current GINA strategy emphasizes ICS-containing treatment rather than SABA-only management for adolescents and adults.

Part 21 — Acute Asthma Assessment

Assess speech, respiratory rate, pulse, oxygenation, accessory muscles, mental status, air movement, and peak flow when feasible without delaying care. A quiet or silent chest, exhaustion, confusion, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, or failure to respond signals life-threatening disease.

Provide rapid bronchodilation, systemic anti-inflammatory therapy and oxygen when indicated according to current protocol, reassess repeatedly, and escalate early. Do not be reassured when wheeze disappears because airflow has become minimal.

Part 22 — COPD Requires Spirometric Confirmation

Consider COPD in persistent dyspnea, chronic cough or sputum, recurrent lower-respiratory events, and exposure to tobacco, biomass, occupational hazards, or other risks. GOLD requires post-bronchodilator spirometry demonstrating persistent airflow obstruction for diagnosis.

Symptoms and exacerbation history guide treatment burden; spirometric grade alone does not describe the whole patient. Consider asthma, heart failure, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, anemia, deconditioning, and lung cancer.

Part 23 — COPD Exacerbation

An exacerbation is acute worsening beyond usual day-to-day variation. Evaluate dyspnea, sputum, oxygenation, work of breathing, mental status, fever, edema, chest pain, and ability to manage at home.

Consider pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, heart failure, arrhythmia, and ACS rather than assuming every deterioration is COPD. Severe hypoxemia, hypercapnia with mental-status change, exhaustion, hemodynamic instability, or failed outpatient care requires emergency evaluation.

Part 24 — Pneumonia: Site and Severity Matter

Fever, cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, focal crackles, hypoxemia, or systemic illness can suggest pneumonia, but presentation may be subtle in older adults. Chest imaging is often used to confirm suspected community-acquired pneumonia when the diagnosis will change management.

Assess severity, comorbidity, oral tolerance, oxygenation, mental status, blood pressure, support, and follow-up. Use a validated severity tool as support, not as a replacement for clinical judgment.

Part 25 — Upper Respiratory Illness and Bronchitis

Most uncomplicated acute bronchitis and viral upper-respiratory syndromes do not benefit from antibiotics. Colored sputum alone does not prove bacterial infection. Provide symptom relief, expected course, infection-control advice, and return precautions.

Reconsider pneumonia, asthma, COPD, pertussis, influenza, COVID-19, or another diagnosis when vital signs, duration, exposure, examination, or risk suggests it. Stewardship is active care, not dismissal.

Part 26 — Chronic Cough

Common contributors include upper-airway cough syndrome, asthma or eosinophilic airway disease, reflux-related mechanisms, ACE-inhibitor use, smoking, chronic lung disease, and environmental exposure. More than one cause may coexist.

Hemoptysis, weight loss, persistent fever, hypoxemia, abnormal imaging, immune compromise, aspiration, occupational risk, or significant smoking history requires focused evaluation. Avoid serial empiric therapy without reassessing the differential.

Part 27 — Hypoxemia and Oxygenation

Confirm signal quality and interpret pulse oximetry with perfusion, movement, nail products, skin pigmentation limitations, altitude, baseline disease, and clinical appearance. A normal number does not exclude hypercapnia; a low number requires assessment of cause and severity.

Supplemental oxygen is a treatment, not the diagnosis. Severe respiratory distress, rapidly falling saturation, cyanosis, altered mentation, or suspected ventilatory failure requires emergency response.

Part 28 — Pleural and Pneumothorax Syndromes

Unilateral pleuritic pain, dyspnea, asymmetric breath sounds, hyperresonance, or risk from trauma, procedures, lung disease, or tall thin body habitus raises concern for pneumothorax. Tension physiology with hypotension, severe distress, and mediastinal pressure is immediately life-threatening.

Pleural effusion can arise from heart failure, infection, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, liver or kidney disease, and other causes. New unexplained or asymmetric effusion generally requires etiologic evaluation.

Part 29 — Sleep-Disordered Breathing

Consider obstructive sleep apnea with snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping, nonrestorative sleep, daytime sleepiness, resistant hypertension, AF, obesity, and craniofacial or upper-airway risk. Use a validated screening tool to estimate risk, not to make the final diagnosis.

Arrange appropriate sleep testing and address driving or occupational safety. Treatment can improve symptoms and may support cardiometabolic and rhythm management.

Part 30 — Tobacco, Vaping, and Exposure

Ask about cigarettes, cigars, pipes, vaping, cannabis inhalation, secondhand smoke, biomass, occupational exposures, and duration. Quantify smoking history when relevant and assess readiness to change without judgment.

Combine behavioral support and evidence-based pharmacotherapy when appropriate. Prevention includes vaccination, lung-cancer screening eligibility, workplace protection, and avoidance of replacing combustible use with ongoing dual use.

Part 31 — Pediatric and Pregnancy Differences

Children have age-specific normal vital signs, airway size, asthma patterns, dosing, and differential diagnoses. Sudden unilateral wheeze suggests foreign-body aspiration. Stridor, drooling, toxic appearance, or fatigue can signal airway emergency.

Pregnancy changes physiology and modifies VTE risk, imaging decisions, medication selection, and thresholds for concern. Do not dismiss dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, severe hypertension, or hypoxemia as normal pregnancy without assessment.

Part 32 — Older Adults and Atypical Presentation

Older adults may present with weakness, falls, delirium, reduced appetite, or functional decline rather than classic chest pain or fever. Polypharmacy, frailty, sensory impairment, kidney dysfunction, aspiration, and baseline cardiopulmonary disease complicate interpretation.

Compare with baseline function and involve caregivers appropriately. Avoid both undertreatment because of age and overtreatment that ignores goals and burden.

Part 33 — Choose Tests That Change Management

ECG, chest radiography, spirometry, echocardiography, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, natriuretic peptide, troponin, D-dimer, CT, and sleep testing answer different questions. Match each test to probability, timing, setting, contraindications, and downstream action.

Do not use D-dimer indiscriminately, order spirometry during severe distress, or wait for outpatient testing when emergency disease is possible. Every abnormal result needs communication and closed-loop follow-up.

Part 34 — Common Board-Style Traps

  • Calling chest pain reflux before excluding high-risk causes
  • Equating a single high blood-pressure value with emergency without assessing organ injury
  • Using one normal troponin or ECG to exclude early ACS
  • Assuming all edema is heart failure or all wheeze is asthma
  • Diagnosing COPD without spirometry
  • Stepping up asthma therapy before checking technique and adherence
  • Using a screening score as a diagnosis
  • Treating viral bronchitis with antibiotics
  • Missing PE, pneumothorax, pneumonia, or HF during a presumed COPD exacerbation
  • Choosing routine follow-up despite instability

Clinical Case 1 — Severe Pressure With Acute Organ Injury

A patient has blood pressure 214/126 mm Hg, severe dyspnea, diffuse crackles, hypoxemia, and confusion.

Reasoning: This is not merely an elevated number. Acute pulmonary edema and neurologic change indicate target-organ injury. Initiate emergency response and transfer for monitored management rather than routine outpatient oral adjustment.

Clinical Case 2 — The Early Normal Troponin

A patient has new resting substernal pressure, diaphoresis, and nausea. The first ECG is nondiagnostic and troponin drawn soon after onset is normal.

Reasoning: Early negative testing does not safely exclude ACS. Continue an validated acute chest-pain pathway with serial ECG and high-sensitivity troponin in an appropriate emergency setting.

Clinical Case 3 — The Quiet Asthma Chest

A patient with asthma is sitting forward, speaking one word at a time, becoming drowsy, and has minimal wheeze with very poor air movement.

Reasoning: Loss of wheeze is not improvement when airflow is critically reduced. This is life-threatening respiratory failure requiring immediate escalation.

Clinical Case 4 — COPD or Something Else?

A patient with COPD develops abrupt pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, new hypoxemia, and unilateral leg swelling after travel.

Reasoning: The abrupt pattern and thrombosis signs suggest pulmonary embolism rather than a routine COPD exacerbation. Use urgent probability-based evaluation and emergency disposition.

Clinical Case 5 — Irregular Rhythm and Stroke Risk

An older adult reports palpitations and dyspnea. ECG confirms AF with a rapid ventricular response, but blood pressure and mentation are stable.

Reasoning: Assess triggers and structural disease, control symptoms and rate or rhythm according to current guidance, and evaluate thromboembolic prevention. Stability permits structured management, but chest pain, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or altered mentation would change urgency.

FNP High-Yield Framework: PULSE-AIR

  1. P — Perfusion and pressure: Blood pressure, pulse, mentation, skin, urine, shock, and target-organ injury.
  2. U — Urgency: Airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, ischemia, arrhythmia, and emergency disposition.
  3. L — Likely syndrome and lethal alternatives: Time course, risks, key positives, key negatives, and competing cardiac-pulmonary causes.
  4. S — Select focused tests: ECG, biomarkers, imaging, spirometry, rhythm or sleep monitoring only when appropriate.
  5. E — Execute initial evidence-based care: Treat the syndrome, avoid contraindications, reassess response, and address triggers.
  6. AIR — Arrange integrated review: Adherence and technique, risk modification, immunization, rehabilitation, referral, follow-up, and return precautions.

Take-Home Summary

Cardiovascular and respiratory symptoms overlap, so begin with airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, perfusion, and stability. For chest pain, consider ACS, aortic syndrome, PE, pneumothorax, tamponade, and esophageal rupture before benign explanations. Interpret severe hypertension by acute target-organ injury, not by the number alone. Recognize heart-failure congestion and hypoperfusion, document arrhythmia before labeling it, assess AF for both symptoms and stroke risk, and treat high-risk syncope urgently. Confirm asthma through variable airflow and COPD through post-bronchodilator obstruction when feasible. During exacerbations, search for mimics and triggers. Evaluate pneumonia severity, avoid antibiotics for uncomplicated viral bronchitis, and never let a normal early test overrule a high-risk clinical pattern. Choose tests that change management, reassess treatment response, and match disposition to risk.

Educational note: This lesson is educational and does not replace emergency assessment, current AHA/ACC, GINA, GOLD, infectious-disease, pulmonary, pediatric, obstetric, or local guidance. Diagnostic thresholds, pathways, and treatments change and must be matched to the patient and clinical setting. Unstable chest pain, respiratory distress, shock, severe hypoxemia, acute neurologic change, or other emergency signs require immediate emergency response.
